title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 2: Prologue to THE COURT BATTLES
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's prologue explaining how, over three years (October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998), he came to argue with almost every member of the Court, and why he regards steadfast dissent as a duty rather than a discourtesy

His personal arc from deference to independence: awed at first by colleagues' lucidity and legal wisdom and inclined to adhere to precedent, he later found that 'being with the majority was not as fulfilling as expressing my thoughts openly and freely according to my best light'

A roll call of his disagreements, dissents received and opinions written -- a case-by-case inventory of who dissented from his ponencias, whose ponencias he concurred in or wrote separately on, and which of his ponencias began in disagreement and ended unanimous

The framing promise for the rest of the book: the celebrated constitutional controversies, plus election, criminal, civil and labor cases, will be summarized from his own viewpoint, with readers referred to the original decisions in the footnotes
sub_topics: The three-year span he is reporting on, in which he discussed and debated questions with almost every member of the Court, and in which members wrote dissenting, concurring or separate opinions on his ponencias

His early deference: awed by the consuming presence of colleagues whose lucidity, legal wisdom and analytical skills he admired, he tended as much as possible to adhere to precedents and conventional doctrines
The turn: he realized that being with the majority was less fulfilling than expressing his thoughts openly and freely according to his best light, regardless of who was on the other side

Justice Isagani A. Cruz's April 4, 1998 column, which noted CJP's Dissent in People v. Montilla and hoped he would see that dissenting 'will not diminish the validity of the dissenter's lonely cause or impair his integrity as a true and thoughtful judge'
His reply to Justice Cruz, the chapter's central line: jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless or thoughtless concurrences
The output statistics he offers as proof of seriousness: 115 to 120 ponencias per year, with separate opinions doubling from 11 in his first two years to 13 in the third year alone
His pledge not to be a fence-sitter or bench warmer in any major battle: he will concur most of the time, but must dissent steadfastly, even if alone, when the need arises

The catalogue of disagreements, justice by justice: with Chief Justice Narvasa on the constitutionality of the Death Penalty Law, with Justice Regalado on illegal arrests and searches, with Justice Davide on the charter change cases, with Justice Romero on the rights of illegitimate children, with Justice Bellosillo on the Filipino First policy, with Justice Puno on the right to privacy, with Justice Vitug on the right of first refusal, with Justice Kapunan on residence as a qualification for congressmen, with Justice Mendoza on the political advertising ban, with Justice Francisco on obedience to a superior's order, and most recently with Justice Purisima on Imelda R. Marcos' acquittal of graft

Dissents written against his own ponencias -- by Justice Davide in Frivaldo v. Comelec and NPC v. Lanao del Sur, Justice Puno in MGG Marine v. NLRC, Justice Vitug in Cabaero v. Cantos and Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Prime Holdings

Concurrences earned by his ponencias (Republic v. Molina, Frivaldo, Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Prime Holdings), the full Concurring Opinions he wrote in Tatad v. Secretary of Energy and People v. Malacat, and the Separate Opinions he penned agreeing with substantial parts of decisions by Justices Puno and Hermosisima

The ponencias that began with dissents or questions and ended in unanimous concurrence -- Tanada v. Angara on the WTO treaty, North Davao Mining on separation pay in distressed companies, Ho v. Sandiganbayan on warrants of arrest, Republic v. Molina on psychological incapacity, and People v. Molina on killing with an illegally possessed firearm -- cases he expects to count among his 'favorite' ones

His closing caveats: the cases that sparked the most opposing opinions were constitutional ones imbued with public interest, and the summaries that follow are written from his viewpoint, with readers advised to consult the original decisions cited in the footnotes

stances.claim: A judge is never diminished by dissenting, only by concurring recklessly or thoughtlessly; a justice must concur most of the time but must dissent steadfastly, even if alone, when the need arises.
stances.rhetorical_move: answers a senior colleague's public encouragement with an epigram that inverts the premise -- the risk lies not in dissent but in unconsidered agreement

stances.claim: Independent judgment is more fulfilling and more proper than adherence to the majority: after an early period of deference to precedent and to his colleagues' stature, he chose to express his thoughts openly and freely according to his best light, regardless of who was on the other side.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-development narrative, offering his own change of habit as the argument

stances.claim: His willingness to dissent is not posturing but is borne out by his record: 115 to 120 ponencias a year with separate opinions doubling from about five or six a year to thirteen in his third year alone.
stances.rhetorical_move: produces his own output statistics as proof against the suspicion of being a fence-sitter

stances.claim: Disagreement in the Court is broad but not personal or partisan: he has differed with virtually every colleague on a different question of law, and several of his ponencias that began in disagreement ended in unanimous concurrence after deliberation.
stances.rhetorical_move: justice-by-justice enumeration, pairing each name with a distinct legal issue rather than a camp

notable_anecdotes: Justice Isagani A. Cruz's April 4, 1998 Inquirer column noticing CJP's dissent in People v. Montilla and hoping he would realize, as Cruz had, that dissenting would not diminish the dissenter's lonely cause -- and CJP's written reply that jurists are diminished only by their reckless or thoughtless concurrences.
His admission that in his first few months he was awed by the consuming presence of colleagues and tended to adhere to precedents and conventional doctrines before finding his own voice.

The 'bit of trivia' he offers Court watchers: separate opinions doubling from eleven in two years to thirteen in his third year alone, as assurance that he would not be a fence-sitter or bench warmer.

His note that several ponencias -- Tanada v. Angara, North Davao Mining, Ho v. Sandiganbayan, Republic v. Molina and People v. Molina -- drew initial dissents or questions that discussion converted into unanimous concurrences, and that he expects to write someday about these 'favorite' cases.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' served as CJP's prologue to the case accounts that follow. Covering his first three years on the Court, from October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1998, he described debating questions with almost every member of the Court and receiving dissenting, concurring and separate opinions on his ponencias. He recounted his own development: in his first months he was awed by the consuming presence of colleagues whose lucidity, legal wisdom and analytical skill he admired, and he tended to adhere to precedents and conventional doctrines, until he realized that being with the majority was not as fulfilling as expressing his thoughts openly and freely according to his best light. He quoted Justice Isagani A. Cruz's April 1998 column, which noted his dissent in People v. Montilla and hoped he would see that dissenting would not diminish the dissenter's cause or his integrity, and gave his reply that jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless or thoughtless concurrences. As evidence that he would not be a fence-sitter or bench warmer, he cited his output of 115 to 120 ponencias a year and the doubling of his separate opinions to thirteen in his third year, pledging to concur most of the time but to dissent steadfastly, even if alone, when the need arose. He then catalogued his disagreements colleague by colleague -- with Narvasa on the Death Penalty Law, Regalado on searches and arrests, Davide on charter change, Romero on illegitimate children, Bellosillo on Filipino First, Puno on privacy, Vitug on the right of first refusal, Kapunan on residence, Mendoza on political advertising, Francisco on obedience to superiors, Purisima on the Marcos acquittal -- then listed the dissents and concurrences his own ponencias drew, and the cases that ended unanimous. He closed by noting that constitutional cases imbued with public interest sparked the most debate, and that his summaries were written from his own viewpoint.
